en.content: If a metal crystallises in bcc structure with edge length of unit cell $4.29 \times 10^{-8} \mathrm{~cm}$ the radius of metal atom is
en.explanation:
In a body-centered cubic (bcc) structure, the relationship between the edge length ($a$) of the unit cell and the radius ($r$) of the metal atom can be derived from the geometry of the structure. The bcc lattice has atoms at each corner of the cube and a single atom at the center.

In a bcc unit cell, the body diagonal of the cube is given by connecting one corner of the cube to the opposite corner through the center atom. The length of the body diagonal in terms of the edge length $a$ is:

$$ \text{body diagonal} = \sqrt{a^2 + a^2 + a^2} = \sqrt{3}a $$

In a bcc structure, this body diagonal is equal to 4 times the radius of the atom ($r$) because it passes through one corner atom, the center atom, and another corner atom. Therefore, we have:

$$ \sqrt{3}a = 4r $$

Solving for the radius $r$:

$$ r = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{4}a $$

Substituting the given edge length $a = 4.29 \times 10^{-8} \, \text{cm}$, we find:

$$ r = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{4} \times 4.29 \times 10^{-8} \, \text{cm} $$

Calculating this gives:

$$ r = \frac{1.732}{4} \times 4.29 \times 10^{-8} \, \text{cm} $$

$$ r \approx 1.86 \times 10^{-8} \, \text{cm} $$

Therefore, the radius of the metal atom is $1.86 \times 10^{-8} \, \text{cm}$.

Option B: $1.86 \times 10^{-8} \text{ cm}$ is the correct answer.

en.content: The integrated rate equation for first order reaction, $A \rightarrow$ product, is
en.explanation:
The integrated rate equation for first order reaction, $A \longrightarrow$ product is $k=-\frac{1}{t} \ln \frac{[A]_t}{[A]_0}$.

For 1st order reactions, $R \longrightarrow P$

$$\text { Rate }=\frac{-d[R]}{d t}=k[R]$$

On integrating this equation, we get

$$\begin{aligned} & \ln [R]=-k t+I \quad\text{.... (i)}\\ & \operatorname{At} t=0, R=[R]_0, \ln [R]_0=-k \times 0+I \\ & \ln [R]_0=I \end{aligned}$$

Substituting the value of $I$ in (i) and on rearrangement, we get

$$\begin{aligned} & \ln [R]=-k t+\ln R_0 \\ & \text { and, } k=\frac{1}{t} \ln \frac{\left[R_0\right]}{[R]} \end{aligned}$$

en.content: Which of the following function has period 2?
en.explanation:
To determine which function has a period of 2, we need to understand the general form of a cosine function and how its period is calculated. The cosine function is periodic, and its standard period is $2\pi$. If a cosine function is given in the form $\cos(bx)$, the period $T$ is calculated using the formula:

$$ T = \frac{2\pi}{|b|} $$

Now let's analyze each option:

Option A:

$\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{3}x\right)$

The period is:

$$ T = \frac{2\pi}{\left|\frac{\pi}{3}\right|} = \frac{2\pi}{\frac{\pi}{3}} = 6 $$

Option B:

$\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{2}x\right)$

The period is:

$$ T = \frac{2\pi}{\left|\frac{\pi}{2}\right|} = \frac{2\pi}{\frac{\pi}{2}} = 4 $$

Option C:

$\cos(2\pi x)$

The period is:

$$ T = \frac{2\pi}{|2\pi|} = 1 $$

Option D:

$\cos(\pi x)$

The period is:

$$ T = \frac{2\pi}{|\pi|} = 2 $$

Thus, the function $\cos(\pi x)$ from Option D is the one with a period of 2.

en.content: The refractive index of the material of crystal is 1.68 and that of castor oil is 1.2. When a ray of light passes from oil to glass, its velocity will change by a factor
en.explanation:
We know, refractive index of crystal w.r.t. oil,

$$\mu_{co}=\frac{\mu_c}{\mu_o}=\frac{\text { speed of light in oil }}{\text { speed of light in crystal }}$$

Where, $\mu_c=$ absolute refractive index of crystal w.r.t. vacuum.

and $\mu_0=$ absolute refractive index of oil w.r.t. vacuum.

$$\mu_{co}=\frac{1.68}{1.2}=\frac{7}{5}=\frac{\text { speed in oil }}{\text { speed in crystal }}$$

Fractional change in velocity, when light travel from oil to crystal

$$=\frac{\text { speed in crystal }}{\text { speed in oil }}=\frac{5}{7}$$

en.content: Consider a particle of mass $m$ suspended by a string at the equator. Let $R$ and $M$ denote radius and mass of the earth. If $\omega$ is the angular velocity of rotation of the earth about its own axis, then the tension on the string will be $\left(\cos 0^{\circ}=1\right)$
en.explanation:
When a body suspended by the string situated at position $P$ as shown in the figure, where latitude is $\lambda$, then body is also rotated with angular frequency $(\omega)$ of earth, hence tension on the string is given by

$$\begin{aligned} & T=m g-m r \omega^2 \cos \lambda \\ T & =m \cdot \frac{G M}{R^2}-m r \omega^2 \cos \lambda\left[\therefore g=\frac{G M}{R^2}\right] \\ T= & \frac{G M m}{R^2}-m r \omega^2 \cos \lambda\quad\text{.... (i)} \end{aligned}$$

When body is suspended at equator, then

$$\lambda=0 \text { and } r=R$$

$\therefore$ From Eq. (i), we have,

$$\begin{aligned} & T=\frac{G M m}{R^2}-m R \omega^2 \cos 0^{\circ} \\ & T=\frac{G M m}{R^2}-m R \omega^2 \end{aligned}$$

en.content: Six very long insulated copper wires are bound together to form a cable. The currents carried by the wires are $I_1=+10 \mathrm{~A}, I_2=-13 \mathrm{~A}, I_3=+10$ $\mathrm{A}, I_4=+7 \mathrm{~A}, I_5=-12 \mathrm{~A}$ and $I_6=+18 \mathrm{~A}$. The magnetic induction at a perpendicular distance of 10 cm from the cable is $\left(\mu_0=4 \pi \times 10^{-7} \mathrm{~Wb} / \mathrm{A}-\mathrm{m}\right)$
en.explanation:
Net current due to all wires,

$$\begin{gathered} i_{\text {net }}=i_1+i_2+i_3+i_4+i_5+i_6 \\ i_{\text {net }}=10-13+10+7-12+18=20 \mathrm{~A} \end{gathered}$$

We know, magnetic field due to an infinitely long straight conductor at a perpendicular distance $r$ from it is given by

$$B=\frac{\mu_0 i}{2 \pi r}=\frac{\mu_0 i_{\text {net }}}{2 \pi r}$$

where, $i=$ current in wire

and $r=$ perpendicular distance.

$$\begin{aligned} & =\frac{4 \pi \times 10^{-7} \times 20}{2 \pi \times 10 \times 10^{-2}}=4 \times 10^{-5} \\ B & =40 \mu \mathrm{~T} \end{aligned}$$

en.content: The fundamental frequency of sonometer wire increases by 9 Hz , if its tension is increased by $69 \%$, keeping the length constant. The frequency of the wire is
en.explanation:
We know that, frequency of vibration of a stretched string is given by

$$\nu=\frac{1}{2} \sqrt{\frac{T}{m}}$$

where, $T=$ tension in string

$m=$ mass / length

and $I=$ length of string.

New frequency,

$$\begin{aligned} & \nu^{\prime}=\nu+9=\frac{1}{2} \sqrt{\frac{T+(69 / 100) T}{m}} \\ & \Rightarrow \quad \frac{\nu}{\nu^{\prime}}=\sqrt{\frac{T}{\frac{T}{109} T}} \Rightarrow \frac{\nu}{\nu+9}=\sqrt{\frac{100}{169}}=\frac{10}{13} \\ & \Rightarrow \quad 13 \nu=10 \nu+90 \\ & \nu=30 \mathrm{~Hz} \end{aligned} $$

en.content: In case of dimensions of electric field and electric dipole moment the power of mass is reswpectively,
en.explanation:
Electric field, $E=\frac{F}{q}$

Where, $F=$ force and $q=$ electric charge

Dimensions of $E$ or $[E]=\frac{\left[\mathrm{ML} \mathrm{T}^{-2}\right]}{[A T]}=\left[\mathrm{ML} \mathrm{T}^{-3} \mathrm{~A}^{-1}\right]$

Power of mass $=1$

Electric dipole moment, $\mathrm{m}=1 \times \mathbf{A}$

where, $I=$ current and $A=$ area

Dimensions of $m=[M]=\left[A L^2\right]=\left[M^0 L^2 T^0 A\right]$

Hence, power of mass $=0$

en.content: A potentiometer wire has length $L$ For given cell of emf $E$, the balancing length is $\frac{L}{3}$ from the positive end of the wire. If the length of potentiometer wire is increased by $50 \%$, then for the same cell, the balance point is obtained at length
en.explanation:
For cell of emf $E$ balancing length $=\frac{L}{3}=\frac{1}{3} \times L($ length of wire $)$

Increased length of wire $=L+\frac{L}{2}=\frac{3 L}{2}$

Since, the cell is the same, therefore the new balancing length $=\frac{1}{3}$ (new increased length)

$$\begin{aligned} & =\frac{1}{3} \times \frac{3}{2} L \\ & =\frac{L}{2} \end{aligned}$$

Therefore, for the same cell the balance point will be as length $\frac{L}{2}$ from positive end.

en.content: For homogeneous isotropic material, which one of the following cannot be the value of Poisson's ratio?
en.explanation:
The Poisson's ratio for homogeneous isotropic material must be between -1.0 to +0.5 because of the requirement. For Young's modulus, the shear modulus and bulk modulus to have positive values.

Hence, 0.8 cannot be the value of Poisson's ratio for homogeneous isotropic material.

en.content: A mass is whirled in a circular path with constant angular velocity and its linear velocity is $v$. If the string is now halved keeping the angular momentum same, the linear velocity is
en.explanation:
Angular velocity $=\omega$

Linear velocity $=v$

Length of string = Radius $=r$

If string is halved, $r^{\prime}=\frac{r}{2}$

Angular momentum, $L=\mathbf{r} \times \mathbf{p}$

where, $\mathbf{r}=$ radius vector and $\mathbf{p}=$ linear momentum.

$$\begin{array}{ll} =r \times m v & {[\because \theta=90^\circ}] \\ =m v r & \end{array}$$

As $L$ remain constant,

$$m v r=\text { constant }$$

$\Rightarrow$ If $r^{\prime} \rightarrow \frac{r}{2}, v^{\prime}=2 v$ such that

$$\begin{aligned} m v^{\prime} r^{\prime} & =m 2 v \times \frac{r}{2} \\ & =m v r \end{aligned}$$

Hence, linear velocity will be $2 v$.

en.content: A circular coil and a square coil is prepared from two identical metal wires and a current is passed through it. Ratio of magnetic dipole moment associated with circular coil to that of square coil is
en.explanation:
Let / be the length of metal wire.

When wire is bent into a circular coil of radius $r$, then

$$\begin{aligned} & r=\frac{1}{2 \pi} \\ \therefore \text{Area},& \qquad A=\pi\left(\frac{1}{2 \pi}\right)^2=\pi \frac{l^2}{4 \pi^2} \end{aligned}$$

$\therefore$ Magnetic dipole moment associated with circular coil,

$$\begin{aligned} & \mu_c=i A=i \pi\left(\frac{l^2}{4 \pi^2}\right) \\ & \mu_c=\frac{i I^2}{4 \pi}\quad\text{.... (i)} \end{aligned}$$

When metal wire is bent into a square coil then side of square

$$a=\frac{I}{4}$$

$\therefore$ Area, $\quad A=a^2=\frac{1^2}{16}$

$\therefore$ Magnetic dipole moment associated with square coil,

$$\begin{aligned} \mu_s=i A & =i \frac{l^2}{16} \\ \therefore\quad\frac{\mu_c}{\mu_s} & =\frac{\frac{i l^2}{4 \pi}}{\frac{1 l^2}{16}}=\frac{16}{4 \pi}=\frac{4}{\pi} \end{aligned}$$

Hence, the ratio of magnetic dipole moment of circular coil and square coil is $4: \pi$.

en.content: In Young's double slit experiment fifth dark fringe is formed opposite to one of the slit. IID is the distance between the slits and the screen and $d$ is the separation between the slits, then the wavelength of light used is
en.explanation:
Position of $n$th dark fringes in Young's double slit experiment is given,

$$\begin{aligned} & x_n=\frac{D}{d}(2 n-1) \frac{\lambda}{2} \\ \lambda= & \frac{2 x_n d}{D(2 n-1)}\quad\text{.... (i)} \end{aligned}$$

Since, fifth dark fringe is formed opposite to one of the slit,

$\therefore 2 x_5=d$ (distance between slits]

Put $n=5$ in Eq. (i), we get

$$\begin{aligned} & \lambda=\frac{2 x_5 d}{D(2 \times 5-1)} \\ & =\frac{d \cdot d}{D(10-1)} \quad \text { [since, } 2 x_5=d] \\ & =\frac{d^2}{9 D} \end{aligned}$$

en.content: Figure show the circular coil carrying current $I$ kept very close but not touching at a point $A$ on a straight conductor carrying the same current $I$. The magnitude of magnetic induction at the centre of the circular coil will be
en.explanation:
Magnetic induction at the centre of circular current carrying loop.

$B_1=\frac{\mu_0 i}{2 r} \quad$ (downward direction)

Magnetic induction at the centre $O$ due to straight wire,

$$B_2=\frac{\mu_0}{2 \pi} \cdot \frac{i}{r}$$ (upward direction)

Net magnetic induction at $O$,

$$\begin{aligned} B & =B_1-B_2=\frac{\mu_0 i}{2 r}-\frac{\mu_0}{2 \pi} \cdot \frac{i}{r} \\ & =\frac{\mu_0 i}{2 r}\left[1-\frac{1}{\pi}\right] \quad \text { [downward direction] } \end{aligned}$$

Hence, there are no option correct.

en.content: A 220 V input is supplied to a transformer. The output circuit draws a current of 2.0 A at 440 V . If the ratio of output to input power is 0.8 , then the current drawn by primary winding is
en.explanation:
Given, input voltage supplied to transformer,

$$V_1=220 \mathrm{~V}$$

Current at output circuit of transformer,

$$\begin{gathered} i_2=2 \mathrm{~A} \\ V_2=440 \mathrm{~V} \\ \frac{\text { Output power }\left(P_2\right)}{\text { Input power }\left(P_1\right)}=0.8 \Rightarrow \frac{V_2 i_2}{V_1 i_1}=0.8 \\ \frac{440 \times 2}{220 \times i_1}=0.8 \\ \frac{4}{i_1}=0.8 \Rightarrow i_1=\frac{4}{0.8}=5 \mathrm{~A} \end{gathered}$$

Hence, current drawn by the primary windings is 5 A .

en.content: A sonometer wire is in unison with a tuning fork, when it is stretched by weight $w$ and the corresponding resonating length is $L_4$. If the weight is reduced to $\left(\frac{w}{4}\right)$, the corresponding resonating length becomes $L_2$. The ratio $\left(\frac{L_1}{L_2}\right)$ is
en.explanation:
When sonometer is stretched by weight $w$ (tension), then frequency of vibration in the string

$$\begin{aligned} & \nu=\frac{1}{2} \sqrt{\frac{T}{m}} \\ & \nu=\frac{1}{2 L_1} \sqrt{\frac{w}{m}}\quad\text{.... (i)} \end{aligned}$$

Where, $L$ is the resonating length and $m$ is mass per unit length of the string.

Similarly, when weight reduces to $\frac{W}{4}$ and resonating length is $L_2$, then

$$\nu=\frac{1}{2 L_2} \sqrt{\frac{\frac{w}{4}}{m}} \Rightarrow v=\frac{1}{4 L_2} \sqrt{\frac{w}{m}}\quad\text{.... (ii)}$$

$$\begin{aligned} &\text { From Eqs. (i) and (ii), we have }\\ &\begin{array}{ll} & \frac{1}{2 L_1} \sqrt{\frac{w}{m}}=\frac{1}{4 L_2} \sqrt{\frac{w}{m}} \Rightarrow L_1=2 L_2 \\ \therefore & \frac{L_1}{L_2}=2 \\ \therefore \quad & L_1: L_2=2: 1 \end{array} \end{aligned}$$

en.content: If the speed of an electron of hydrogen atom in the ground state is $2.2 \times 10^6 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$, then its speed in the third excited state will be
en.explanation:
Speed of electron of hydrogen atom in ground state,

$$\begin{aligned} & v_1=22 \times 10^6 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s} \\ & \text { Since, } \quad v \propto \frac{1}{n} \\ & \therefore \quad \frac{v_1}{v_2}=\frac{n_2}{n_1}=\frac{2.2 \times 10^6}{v_2} \\ & \text { [for third excited state, } n_2=4 \text { ] } \\ & \Rightarrow \quad v_2=\frac{2.2 \times 10^6}{4}=0.55 \times 10^6 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s} \\ & =5.5 \times 10^5 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s} \end{aligned}$$

en.content:
A rod $l \mathrm{~m}$ long is acted upon by a couple as shown in the figure. The moment of couple is $\tau \mathrm{~Nm}$. If the force at each end of the rod, then magnitude of each force is

$$\left(\sin 30^{\circ}=\cos 60^{\circ}=0.5\right)$$
en.explanation:
Length of rod = $l$

Moment of couple,

$$\begin{aligned} & \tau=Fl \sin \theta \\ \therefore & F=\frac{\tau}{l \sin \theta}=\frac{\tau}{l \sin 30^{\circ}}=\frac{\tau}{l \times \frac{1}{2}} \end{aligned}$$

Force, $\quad F=\frac{2 \tau}{l}$

en.content: The vectors $(\mathbf{A}+\mathbf{B})$ and $(\mathbf{A}-\mathbf{B})$ are at right. angles to each other. This is possible under the condition
en.explanation:
Vectors $(\mathbf{A}+\mathbf{B})$ and $(\mathbf{A}-\mathbf{B})$ are at right angle to each other, therefore

$$\begin{aligned} & (A+B) \cdot(A-B)=0 \\ & A \cdot A+B \cdot A-A \cdot B-B \cdot B=0 \\ & |A|+B A \cos \theta-A B \cos \theta-|B|^2=0 \\ & |A|^2=|B|^2 \\ \text{Hence,}\quad& |A|=|B| \end{aligned}$$

en.content: A coil has inductance 2 H . The ratio of its reactance, when it is connected first to an $A C$ source and then to DC source, is
en.explanation:
Given, inductance of a coil, $L=2 \mathrm{H}$

Reactance of coil, when it is connected to $A C$ source,

$$\begin{aligned} & \left(X_L\right)_{A C}=\frac{1}{\omega L} \text { where, } \omega=\text { angular frequency } \\ & \left(X_L\right)_\omega=\frac{1}{2 \mu \omega} \end{aligned}$$

For DC source, inductor coil behaves as pure conductor, hence $\left(X_L\right)_{\mathrm{DC}}=0$

$$\therefore \quad \frac{\left(X_L\right)_{A C}}{\left(X_L\right)_{D C}}=\frac{\frac{1}{2 \omega}}{0}=\infty\quad\text{(at infinity)}$$

en.content: A person measures a time period of a simple pendulum inside a stationary lift and finds it to be $T$. If the lift starts accelerating upwards with an acceleration $\left(\frac{g}{3}\right)$, the time period of the pendulum will be
en.explanation:
Time period of simple pendulum inside a stationary lift,

$$T=2 \pi \sqrt{\frac{l}{g}}\quad\text{.... (i)}$$

where, $I=$ length of string

and $g=$ gravitational acceleration

Acceleration of lift in upward direction,

$$a=\frac{g}{3}$$

$\therefore$ Time period of pendulum,

$$\begin{aligned} \text { d of pendulum, } \\ \begin{aligned} T^{\prime} & =2 \pi \sqrt{\frac{l}{g+a}}=2 \pi \sqrt{\frac{l}{g+\frac{g}{3}}} \\ & =2 \pi \sqrt{\frac{3l}{4 g}}=2 \pi \cdot \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \cdot \sqrt{\frac{l}{g}} \\ & =\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \cdot 2 \pi \sqrt{\frac{l}{g}}=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} T \text { [from Eq. (i)] } \end{aligned} \end{aligned}$$

en.content: A charged conductor produces an electric field of intensity $10^3 \mathrm{~V} / \mathrm{m}$ just outside its surface in vacuum. Then, it produces the electric field of intensity E just outside its surface, when it is placed in a medium of dielectric constant 4. The value of $E$ will be
en.explanation:
Given, electric field produced by charged conductor in vacuum,

$$E_0=10^3 \mathrm{~V} / \mathrm{m}$$

Electric field produced by charged conductor, when it is placed in medium of dielectrics $(K=4)$ is $E=\frac{E_0}{K}=\frac{10^3}{4}=250 \mathrm{~V} / \mathrm{m}$

en.content: In damped SHM, the SI unit of damping constant is
en.explanation:
In damped SHM, damping force is proportional to the velocity of the oscillator.

i.e., $$F_d \propto v \Rightarrow F_d=b v$$

where, $b$ is a damping constant.

$\therefore$ Damping constant, $b=\frac{F_d}{v}$

SI unit of damping constant

$$\begin{aligned} b & =\frac{\text { SI unit of force }}{\text { SI unit of velocity }}=\frac{\mathrm{kg} \cdot \mathrm{~m} \cdot \mathrm{~s}^{-2}}{\mathrm{~m} \cdot \mathrm{~s}^{-1}} \\ & =\mathrm{kg} \cdot \mathrm{~s}^{-1}=\frac{\mathrm{kg}}{\mathrm{~s}} \end{aligned}$$

Hence, the SI unit of damping constant is $\mathrm{kg} / \mathrm{s}$.

en.content: A wire of length $L$ and radius $r$ is rigidly fixed at one end. On stretching the other end of the wire with a force $F$, the increase in length is $I$. If another wire of the same material but double the length and radius is stretched with a force $2 F$, then increase in length is
en.explanation:
Let the length of wire $=L$

Radius $=r$

When a force $F$ is applied, then increase in length = ($l$).

Since, Young's modulus

$$Y=\frac{\frac{F}{\pi r^2}}{\frac{1}{L}} \Rightarrow Y=\frac{F L}{\pi r^2 I}\quad\text{... (i)}$$

For another wire,

length of wire, $L^{\prime}=2 L$

Radius of wire, $r^{\prime}=2 r$

$$\begin{aligned} & \text { Applied force, } F^{\prime}=2 F \\ & \qquad \begin{aligned} \quad & =\frac{F^{\prime} L^{\prime}}{\pi r^2 l^{\prime}} \text { where, } l^{\prime}=\text { elongation in length } \\ & =\frac{2 F \cdot 2 L}{\pi(2 r)^2 \cdot l^{\prime}}=\frac{4 F L}{4 \pi r^2 l^{\prime}} \\ Y & =\frac{F L}{\pi r^2 l^{\prime}}\quad\text{.... (ii)} \end{aligned} \end{aligned}$$

From Eqs. (i) and (ii), we have $l'=l$

en.content: When certain metal surface is illuminated with a light of wavelength $\lambda$, the stopping potential is $V$, When the same surface is illuminated by light of wavelength $2 \lambda$, the stopping potential is $\left(\frac{V}{3}\right)$. The threshold wavelength for the surface is
en.explanation:
Given for a metal, wavelength of light used $=\lambda$

Stopping potential $=V$

If $\lambda_0$ be the threshold wavelength, then maximum kinetic energy of emitted electrons

$K_{\max }=h c\left(\frac{1}{\lambda}-\frac{1}{\lambda_0}\right)\quad\text{.... (i)}$

Again, wavelength of used light

$$\lambda^{\prime}=2 \lambda$$

Stopping potential, $V^{\prime}=\frac{V}{3}$

then $$K_{\max }=h c\left(\frac{1}{\lambda^{\prime}}-\frac{1}{\lambda_0}\right)$$

$$\begin{array}{ll} \Rightarrow & e V^{\prime}=h c\left(\frac{1}{2 \lambda}-\frac{1}{\lambda_0}\right) \\ \Rightarrow & \frac{e V}{3}=h c\left(\frac{1}{2 \lambda}-\frac{1}{\lambda_0}\right)\quad\text{.... (ii)} \end{array}$$

From Eqs. (i) and (ii), we have

$$\begin{array}{r} \frac{e V}{\frac{e V}{3}}=\frac{h c\left(\frac{1}{\lambda}-\frac{1}{\lambda_0}\right)}{h c\left(\frac{1}{2 \lambda}-\frac{1}{\lambda_0}\right)} \\ 3\left(\frac{1}{2 \lambda}-\frac{1}{\lambda_0}\right)=\frac{1}{\lambda}-\frac{1}{\lambda_0}\\ \Rightarrow \lambda_0=4\lambda \end{array}$$

So, threshold wavelength is 4 times of wavelengths of light.

en.content: Which of the following regions of a transistors are, respectively, heavily dopped and lightly dopped?
en.explanation:
In a transistor, emitter region is highly doped because it injects charge carriers toward base and collector region.

Collector region is moderately doped because in recombination of charge carriers takes place in this region.

Base region are lightly doped, so that recombination of charge carriers is small.

en.content: A hole is drilled half way to the centre of the earth. A body weighs 300 N on the surface of the earth. How much will, it weigh at the bottom of the hole?
en.explanation:
Given, distance of bottom of hole from the surface of earth $(d)=$ half the radius of earth $=\frac{R_e}{2}$

If $g$ be the value of gravitational acceleration on the surface of earth, then weight of body

$$m g=300 \mathrm{~N}$$

If $g^{\prime}$ be the gravitational acceleration at the bottom of hole, then

$$g^{\prime}=g\left(1-\frac{d}{R_\theta}\right)=g\left(1-\frac{\frac{R_\theta}{2}}{R_e}\right) \Rightarrow g^{\prime}=\frac{g}{2}$$

$\therefore$ Weight of the body on the bottom of hole,

$$m g^{\prime}=\frac{m g}{2}=\frac{300}{2}=150 \mathrm{~N}$$

en.content: Eight identical drops of water falling through air with uniform velocity of $10 \mathrm{~cm} / \mathrm{s}$ combine to form a single drop of big size, then terminal velocity of the big drop will be
en.explanation:
Given, terminal velocity of each small drop

$$v_1=10 \mathrm{~cm} / \mathrm{s}$$

When 8 small drops are combined to form bigger drop, then volume will be same.

If $r_1$ be radius of small drop and $r_2$ be radius of bigger drop, then $v_2=v_1$

$$\frac{4}{3} \pi r_2^3=8 \times \frac{4}{3} \pi r_1^3 \Rightarrow r_2=2 r_1$$

$\therefore$ Terminal velocity of the drop

$$\begin{aligned} & v=\frac{2}{9} \frac{r^2(\rho-\sigma)}{9 \eta} \\ \text{i.e.,}\quad & v \propto r^2 \\ \therefore\quad& \frac{v_1}{v_2}=\frac{r_1^2}{r_2^2}=\frac{r_1^2}{\left(2 r_1\right)^2} \Rightarrow \frac{v_1}{v_2}=\frac{1}{4} \\ & v_2=4 v_1=4 \times 10=40 \mathrm{~cm} / \mathrm{s}\end{aligned}$$

en.content: A solid sphere rolls down from top of inclined plane, 7 m high, without slipping. Its linear speed at the foot of plane is $\left(g=10 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}^2\right)$
en.explanation:
Given, height of inclined plane, $h=7 \mathrm{~m}$

$$g=10 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}^2$$

By conservation of energy,

Potential energy lost by the solid sphere in rolling down the inclined plane $=$ Kinetic energy gained by the sphere.

$$\begin{aligned} m g h & =\frac{1}{2} m v^2+\frac{1}{2} l \omega^2 \\ & =\frac{1}{2} m v^2+\frac{1}{2} \cdot \frac{2}{5} m R^2 \cdot\left(\frac{v}{R}\right)^2 \\ & =\frac{1}{2} m v^2+\frac{1}{5} m v^2 \\ m g h & =\frac{7}{10} m v^2 \\ \therefore \quad v^2 & =\frac{10}{7} g h \\ \Rightarrow \quad v & =\sqrt{\frac{10}{7} g h}=\sqrt{\frac{10}{7} \times 10 \times 7}=\sqrt{100} \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s} \end{aligned}$$

en.content: A body of mass $m$ is performing a UCM in a circle of radius $r$ with speed $v$. The work done by the centripetal force in moving it through $\left(\frac{2}{3}\right) \mathrm{rd}$ of the circular path is
en.explanation: When a body perform uniform circular motion, then centripetal force acts always in perpendicular direction to its velocity, hence work done by centripetal force is always zero. Hence, work done by centripetal force is zero, when it through $\left(\frac{2}{3}\right)$ rd of the circular path.

en.content: Which of the following is the dimensional formula for electric polarisation?
en.explanation:
Electric polarisation $(P)$ is given by

$$P=\varepsilon_0 \chi E$$

where, $E$ is electric field and $\chi$ is electric susceptibility and it is dimensionless quantity,

Dimensional formula of $P=$ Dimensional formula of $\left(\varepsilon_0\right) \times$ Dimensional formula of $E$

$$=\left[M^{-1} L^{-3} T^4 I^2\right]\left[M L T^{-3} I^{-1}\right]=\left[M^0 L^{-2} T^1 I^1\right]$$

en.content: The phenomenon of interference is based on
en.explanation: In interference phenomenon, energy is distributed such that intensity of resultant wave is maximum at some points and minimum at another points, therefore phenomenon of interference is based on conservation of energy.

en.content: A vector $P$ has $X$ and $Y$ components of magnitude 2 units and 4 units respectively. A vector $Q$ along negative $X$-axis has magnitude 6 units. The vector $(\mathbf{Q}-\mathbf{P})$ will be
en.explanation:
According to question, vectors $\mathbf{P}$ and $\mathbf{Q}$ can be written as

$$\begin{array}{rlrl} & \mathbf{P} =2 \hat{\mathbf{i}}+4 \hat{\mathbf{j}} \\ \text { and } & \quad \mathbf{Q} =-6 \hat{\mathbf{i}} \\ \therefore & \mathbf{Q}-\mathbf{P} =-6 \hat{\mathbf{i}}-(2 \hat{\mathbf{i}}+4 \hat{\mathbf{j}}) \\ & =-8 \hat{\mathbf{i}}-4 \hat{\mathbf{j}}=-4(2 \hat{\mathbf{i}}+\hat{\mathbf{j}}) \end{array}$$

en.content: A magnetizing field of $5000 \mathrm{~A} / \mathrm{m}$ produces a magnetic flux of $4 \times 10^{-5} \mathrm{~Wb}$ in an iron rod of cross-sectional area $0.4 \mathrm{~cm}^2$. The permeabilit of the rod in Wb/A-m, is
en.explanation:
Given, magnetising field, $H=5000 \mathrm{~A} / \mathrm{m}$

Magnetic flux, $\phi=4 \times 10^{-5} \mathrm{~Wb}$

Cross-sectional area, $A=0.4 \mathrm{~cm}^2=4 \times 10^{-5} \mathrm{~m}^2$

$\therefore$ Permeability of rod,

$$\begin{aligned} \mu & =\frac{B}{H}=\frac{\phi}{A H} \quad \quad\left[\therefore \phi=B A \Rightarrow B=\frac{\phi}{A}\right] \\ & =\frac{4 \times 10^{-5}}{4 \times 10^{-5} \times 5000}=2 \times 10^{-4} \mathrm{~Wb} / \mathrm{A}-\mathrm{m} \end{aligned}$$

en.content: When a large bubble rises from bottom of a water lake to its surface, then its radius doubles. If the atmospheric pressure is equal to the pressure of height $H$ of a certain water column, then the depth of lake will be
en.explanation:
When a large bubble rises from bottom of water lake to its surface, then its radius becomes double.

$$\text { i.e., } \quad r_2=2 r_1$$

Since, volume $V \propto r^3$

$$\begin{array}{ll} \therefore & \frac{V_2}{V_1}=\left(\frac{r_2}{r_1}\right)^3=\left(\frac{2 r_1}{r_1}\right)^3=8 \\ \Rightarrow & V_2=8 V_1\quad\text{... (i)} \end{array}$$

From Boyle's law,

$$p_1 V_1=p_2 V_2$$

Where, $p_2=$ atmospheric pressure.

$p_1 V_1=p_2 8V_1$ [From Eq. (i)]

$$p_2=\frac{p_1}{8}\quad\text{.... (ii)}$$

Where, $p_2=$ atmospheric pressure and $p_1=$ pressure at depth $d$.

$$\begin{aligned} \therefore \quad & p_1=p_{\text {atmospheric }}+\rho g d \\ p_1 & =p_2+\rho g d\quad\text{.... (iii)} \end{aligned}$$

From Eqs. (ii) and (iii), we have

$$\begin{gathered} p_2=\frac{p_2+\rho g d}{8} \\ 7 p_2=\rho g d \\ 7 \cdot \rho g H=\rho g d \\ 7 H=d \Rightarrow d=7 H \end{gathered}$$

en.content: In hydrogen emission spectrum, for any series, the principal quantum number is $n$. Corresponding maximum wavelength $\lambda$ is ( $R=$ Rydberg's constant)
en.explanation:
In hydrogen emission spectrum, wavelength is given by

$$\frac{1}{\lambda}=R\left(\frac{1}{n_1^2}-\frac{1}{n_2^2}\right)$$

For maximum wavelength of any principal quantum number $n$,

$$\begin{aligned} & n_1=n \text { and } n_2=n+1 \\ \therefore\quad & \frac{1}{\lambda_{\max }}=R\left[\frac{1}{n^2}-\frac{1}{(n+1)^2}\right] \\ & =R\left[\frac{(n+1)^2-n^2}{n^2(n+1)^2}\right] \\ & =R \frac{\left(n^2+2 n+1-n^2\right)}{n^2(n+1)^2} \\ & \frac{1}{\lambda_{\max }}=\frac{R^2(2 n+1)}{n^2(n+1)^2} \\ & \therefore \quad \lambda_{\max }=\frac{n^2(n+1)^2}{R(2 n+1)} \end{aligned}$$

en.content: If the radius of the circular path and frequency of revolution of a particle of mass $m$ are doubled, then the change in its kinetic energy will be $\left(E_i\right.$ and $E_1$ are the initial and final kinetic energies of the particle respectively,)
en.explanation:
Initial kinetic energy of body,

$$\begin{aligned} & E_i=\frac{1}{2} m v^2=\frac{1}{2} m\left(\frac{2 \pi r_1}{T_1}\right)^2\left[\because v=\frac{2 \pi r}{T}\right] \\ & E_i=2 \pi^2 m r_1^2 f_1^2\quad\text{.... (i)} \end{aligned}$$

Where, $f_1=$ frequency of revolution of the body.

$$\begin{aligned} \text{When, }\quad r_2 & =2 r_1 \text { and } f_2=2 f_1 \text {, then } \\ E_f & =2 \pi^2 m \cdot r_2^2 \cdot f_2^2 \\ & =2 \pi^2 m\left(2 r_1\right)^2\left(2 f_1\right)^2 \\ E_f & =32 \pi^2 m r_1^2 f_1^2=16 \cdot 2 \pi^2 m r_1^2 f_1^2 \\ E_f & =16 E_i \end{aligned}$$

$\therefore$ Change in kinetic energy,

$$\begin{aligned} \Delta E & =E_i-E_i \\ & =16 E_i-E_i=15 E_i \end{aligned}$$

en.content: The rms speed of oxygen molecule in a gas is $u$, If the temperature is doubled and the molecules dissociates into two atoms, the rms speed will be
en.explanation:
To determine the new root mean square (rms) speed of the oxygen molecules when the temperature is doubled and they dissociate into atoms, we can use the formula for the rms speed:

$$ v_{\text{rms}} = \sqrt{\frac{3kT}{m}} $$

where:

$ v_{\text{rms}} $ is the root mean square speed,

$ k $ is the Boltzmann constant,

$ T $ is the temperature,

$ m $ is the mass of a molecule.

Initially, the oxygen molecule ($ O_2 $) has a mass $ m $, and its rms speed is $ u $. Therefore:

$$ u = \sqrt{\frac{3kT}{M}} $$

where $ M $ is the molar mass of the oxygen molecule $ O_2 $.

When the temperature is doubled ($ T' = 2T $), and oxygen molecules dissociate into atoms, the mass of an individual oxygen atom is $ \frac{M}{2} $. The new rms speed $ u' $ can be calculated as:

$$ u' = \sqrt{\frac{3k(2T)}{\frac{M}{2}}} $$

This simplifies to:

$$ u' = \sqrt{\frac{6kT}{\frac{M}{2}}} = \sqrt{\frac{6kT \cdot 2}{M}} = \sqrt{\frac{12kT}{M}} = \sqrt{4 \cdot \frac{3kT}{M}} $$

The term $\frac{3kT}{M}$ corresponds to the square of the initial rms speed, $ u^2 $:

$$ u' = \sqrt{4} \cdot u = 2u $$

Thus, the new rms speed will be $ 2u $. Therefore, the correct answer is:

Option C: 2u.
